title: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (6 of 7)
hook: a ghost, a dog's curly tail, and why you can't fix the world
tomorrow: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (7 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: svakarmana, with your own work, worship. Offered work is careful work.

A year of volunteering, donating, showing up for the cause, and the problem looks exactly the same. The shelter is still full. The inbox is still full. And a quiet voice asks: what's the point? Vivekananda took that question seriously. In his Karma Yoga lectures he answered it with a strange little story about a man, a ghost, and a dog's tail that would not stay straight. The chapter's title sounds almost rude: We Help Ourselves, Not the World.
screen: `THE PROBLEM LOOKS THE SAME.` → `WHAT'S THE POINT?` → `WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Vivekananda tells it. A man wanted a ghost to do his work for him, and he got one. But there was a catch: the ghost had to be kept busy every minute, or it would kill him. It finished every job in no time. Build a house: done. Clear a field: done. The man, terrified, ran to a wise teacher, who said: tell it to straighten a dog's curly tail. The ghost pulled the tail straight. Let go, and it curled back up. Pulled again. Curled. That kept it busy. The world, Vivekananda said, is like that dog's tail. People keep pulling it straight; let go, and it curls. So is helping pointless? No. That's the turn. When we help, he said, we're not fixing the world. The world will go on. We are the ones being changed. So, he said, be grateful to the person you help: they gave you the chance. Then the second half: work like a master, not a slave. A slave works for the reward, and is crushed when it doesn't come. A master works freely, because the work is worth doing. The Gita has a picture for it: the one who acts, offering the action and letting go of attachment, isn't stained by it, the way a lotus leaf sits in water and stays dry. The tail still curls. You keep straightening it anyway, and you stay dry.
screen: `A GHOST THAT MUST BE KEPT BUSY.` · `THE WORLD IS A DOG'S CURLY TAIL.` · `THE HELPER IS THE ONE WHO CHANGES.` · `A LOTUS LEAF IN THE WATER.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you keep trying to fix that keeps curling back: a cause, a messy house, a relative who won't change. Breathe in and feel how much you want the result; breathe out and set the result down beside you, just for now. Then picture doing the next small piece anyway, because it's worth doing, like the lotus leaf: in the water, and dry.
Master, one who works freely, not for reward. We help ourselves, not the world: the work changes the worker. Stay dry like the lotus leaf, unattached to the result.
Your line: offer the work. The tail still curls, and the helper still grows. Day two hundred sixty-five, done.

howItsDone: In seva, service offered freely, many Hindus aim to help without clinging to results or credit, often using the Gita's image of the lotus leaf that sits in water without getting wet.

fork.setup: you're the man. the ghost has finished every job, and it will kill you if it's idle. what does the teacher tell you?
options: have it straighten a dog's curly tail.
give it a very big house to build.
fork.reveal: the curly tail: pulled straight, it curls back, forever. Vivekananda's picture of the world, and of work that never ends.

original.note: Sanskrit, Gita 5.10: 'like a lotus leaf by water' — untouched by what it sits in.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma yoga is about fixing the world through good works.
what it means: the work is worth doing, but its deepest effect is on the one who does it, freely and without clinging.

what a scholar hears: Vivekananda's 'we help ourselves, not the world' reframes service as spiritual discipline; the lotus-leaf image is Gita 5.10 (padmapatram ivāmbhasā), a common picture in Indian texts for being in the world without being stained by it.

a boss who has others do the work for him
an expert who has perfected a craft
recall: a twelve-verse Upanishad all about om
a sacred fig tree, pictured upside down

chat.says: I keep helping, and nothing really changes. What's the point?
options: Vivekananda says helping changes the helper, even if the world stays the same.
There isn't one; the world is a curly tail, so it's fine to stop.
Keep pulling, and one day the world will stay straight for good.
chat.meaning: The dog's tail curls back, but we help ourselves: the work changes the worker. So keep working, like a master, unattached.

Vivekananda.meaning: Hindu monk who taught in America; author of Karma Yoga

Karma Yoga.meaning: the path of action done as an offering

Gita.meaning: the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna
